newsitem.title: JAPAN: JGBs advance into uncharted waters by late Tokyo.
newsitem.headline: JGBs advance into uncharted waters by late Tokyo.

text.p: Cash Japanese government bonds (JGB) extended gains into uncharted waters with the benchmark yield falling to a record low 2.350 percent in a buying spree led by both investors and dealers, traders said on Monday.
"Even before the opening, the market was strongly tapped by substantial buying orders from trust banks, pension funds and public funds, promising a bull run during the day," said a city bank trader.
The yield of the 182nd 10-year JGB set a new historical low of 2.350 percent, the lowest ever for any key cash issue, by late Tokyo trading, down from 2.415 percent on Friday.

Japan's economic recovery appears to be becoming more solid, as seen in the central bank's "tankan" survey released last Wednesday, Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita told a news conference on Monday.
Traders said Matsushita's remark was bearish for bonds, but the dive in Tokyo stocks immediately after the remark effectively offset downward pressure on bonds.
The decline in Tokyo stocks led bond traders to anticipate more cash flows into bonds in a "flight to quality".
The new key March JGB contract ended sharply higher at 126.28, compared with Friday's 125.53 finish.

Matsushita said the central bank's easy money policy was intended to prevent a deflationary spiral, to strengthen corporate confidence and to put the economy back on a self-sustainable recovery track. He said the first two aims had "just about been achieved".

"Compared with the economic assessment held by the BOJ or other government officials, the market outlook on the economy is comparatively pessimistic, or perhaps too much so," said another city bank official. But he said this perception gap was unavoidable to some extent because market players are mostly financial institutions which face a not too bright future.
Meanwhile, foreign speculative accounts unloaded Tokyo stock futures and bought JGB futures, accentuating the gains in the JGBs, some traders said.
These accounts were making fresh long positions in the new benchmark March, while unloading the December, which is due to expire on December 9, they said.
Some said that the long end of the cash JGBs, which had been slow to catch up with the medium-term sector, were quickly narrowing the gap through an advance on Monday.
